vignette: Maria, a 70-year-old widowed European woman and retired hotel manager, has been struggling with the aftermath of an incident involving police violence that occurred several months ago. The event remains vividly etched in her mind, and she continues to be plagued by intrusive thoughts about what happened, particularly around anniversaries and when she finds herself in crowded places. The day of the traumatic event was a regular workday at the hotel where Maria worked as manager. She had just finished organizing an important conference when several police officers arrived unannounced, ostensibly to conduct routine checks. As they proceeded through the building, their aggressive demeanor quickly escalated tensions. One officer confronted Maria in a crowded hallway, and his threatening behavior triggered her immediate fear response. The situation rapidly deteriorated into a violent confrontation, leaving Maria shaken and traumatized. Since then, Maria has found herself constantly on edge, especially around anniversaries of the event. On those days, intrusive thoughts flood her mind, often without warning, evoking the same terror she felt during the incident. These triggers are particularly potent because they remind her of the vivid details of that day—the aggressive mannerisms of the officer, the fear in the eyes of other hotel staff, and the overall chaos. Maria’s memories of the event are so detailed and clear that they often surface spontaneously. Even mundane occurrences can instantly bring back the full memory with the same intensity as if she were reliving it. This triggered recall is particularly distressing because it reinforces her negative appraisals about herself and institutions meant to protect her. She has come to believe that those who should have safeguarded her failed miserably, leaving her feeling like a stranger in her own skin. The memory’s clarity and the vividness of the experience contribute significantly to Maria's growing sense of institutional failure and identity loss. Remembering the event brings back not only the terror but also the realization that she has permanently changed for the worse. She feels as though the trauma has irrevocably altered who she is, leaving her questioning her own stability and worth. Maria’s negative appraisals have deepened over time, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of fear and doubt. The clarity of her memories serves to solidify her belief that the institutions meant to protect her let her down, further exacerbating her sense of permanent damage. She has begun to avoid crowded places entirely, finding it difficult to engage in activities she once enjoyed. Maria’s avoidance behaviors have had concrete consequences both professionally and personally. As a hotel manager, dealing with crowds is part of daily life, but the trauma has made this aspect of her job nearly unbearable. Her interactions with staff and guests are strained, as she often finds herself withdrawing from situations that trigger unwanted memories. This withdrawal has led to a noticeable decline in her work performance and has affected her relationships with colleagues. Maria’s current state is marked by an overwhelming sense of helplessness and fear. She realizes that the trauma is affecting every aspect of her life but struggles to manage the constant reminders and triggers. It was only when she found herself unable to leave her apartment for several days, overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts and memories, that she finally decided to seek professional help. What frightens Maria most is the prospect of living with these persistent fears indefinitely—of never feeling safe or secure again. She hopes to regain a sense of stability and control over her life, free from the constant reminders of the traumatic event and its aftermath.
